query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (HEA), service‐relevant cyclic or elevated temperature loading induces a local, stress‐assisted short‐range atomic ordering (or subtle elemental partitioning) at grain boundaries that effectively reduces the grain boundary cohesive strength and leads to an incipient brittle behavior even in the absence of conventional brittle grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase, fine‐grained HEA with uniform elemental distribution and high intrinsic toughness (e.g., an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi or similar composition) as produced by equilibrium processing.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled in‐service loading conditions—either cyclic deformation or elevated temperature aging (or both) that simulate extended engineering service.
generation.conditions: Testing at temperatures in the intermediate-to-high service range (e.g., 600–700°C) and/or under repeated cyclic mechanical loading (with strain amplitudes typical of service) while comparing with a baseline held at room temperature under static load.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of localized short‐range ordering or incipient segregation at or near grain boundaries without full intermetallic precipitation.
generation.mechanism: Under extended cyclic and/or elevated temperature conditions, the HEA’s inherent sluggish diffusion combined with high local strain fields promotes limited atomic reordering or elemental redistribution particularly at areas of stress concentration such as grain boundaries. This dynamic rearrangement, although not producing bulk precipitates, reduces intergranular cohesion and thus lowers the effective toughness, leading to a transition from ductile transgranular fracture to brittle intergranular fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline samples maintained under mild conditions, loaded samples will exhibit (a) detectable local changes in grain boundary chemistry or short‐range order (via APT or high-resolution TEM) and (b) a shift in fracture mode toward intergranular, accompanied by a measurable reduction in fracture toughness (e.g., lower critical resolved shear stress for intergranular crack initiation or reduced bending/tensile ductility).
generation.baseline: As-processed, fully homogeneous single-phase HEA samples exhibiting ductile, transgranular fracture behavior with high toughness under low-temperature and static loading conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to become significant under service conditions where the temperature and/or cyclic stress is high enough to promote observable atomic rearrangements at grain boundaries but below the threshold for full-scale recrystallization or bulk precipitate formation; the effect is anticipated for materials with grain sizes and compositions typical of engineering HEAs used in demanding environments.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of short-range order formation, its exact influence on intergranular cohesion, and the critical loading/temperature thresholds for its onset are not yet precisely known and will require detailed atomistic and statistical investigations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical, as-cast single-phase HEA specimens. Subject one set to accelerated service-simulated conditions—cyclic mechanical loading at an elevated temperature (e.g., 650°C with controlled strain amplitudes) for an extended period, while maintaining a control set at room temperature under static load. Following exposure, perform high-resolution atom probe tomography (APT) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) at grain boundaries to assess any development of short-range atomic ordering or elemental partitioning. Conduct fracture toughness measurements (e.g., bend tests or micro-tensile tests) and fractographic analysis (via SEM) to determine if there is a shift from transgranular to intergranular fracture mode.
measurements: APT/TEM analysis of grain boundary chemistry and ordering
Fracture toughness testing (e.g., critical stress intensity factor)
SEM fractography to distinguish intergranular vs. transgranular fracture
Mechanical property measurements (yield strength, elongation) under quasi-static conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclic/elevated temperature-treated specimens show no detectable change in grain boundary ordering or elemental segregation relative to the control, and if fracture mode and toughness remain statistically identical to the baseline, then the hypothesis—that service loading induces stress-driven grain boundary reordering leading to embrittlement—will be falsified.

Question: How does the combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering affect the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of an equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy, particularly regarding the formation of secondary phases due to interstitial elements?. System: Equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (Nb: 16.67 at%, Mo: 16.67 at%, Ta: 16.67 at%, W: 16.67 at%, V: 16.67 at%, Ti: 16.67 at%) with oxygen introduction. Processing: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders (≥99.9% purity) in a high energy planetary ball mill with stainless steel balls/vial at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 13:1 under high purity argon for 40 h; followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of the 40 h milled powders in a graphite die at 1400 °C for 10 min under 30 MPa pressure, with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and cooling to 500 °C at 300 °C/min. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ on cylindrical samples (Φ3 mm × 6 mm); density measured by Archimedes' method; microstructure analyzed via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EDS.
